'''Hyman Garshin Landau''' (December 18, 1909 – December 2, 1966), more often known as '''H. G. Landau''', was an American [[mathematical biologist]], [[statistician]] and [[Sociology|sociologist]] who is known for using mathematical methods such as [[graph theory]] to understand [[Ethology|animal behavior]] and [[social dynamics]]. After receiving his [[doctorate]] in [[statistics]] from the [[University of Pittsburgh]], he worked at the [[Ballistic Research Laboratory]] at [[Aberdeen Proving Ground]], [[Maryland]], while teaching part-time at the [[University of Delaware]]. He carried out his seminal work on [[Tournament (graph theory)|graph tournaments]] as a research associate at the [[University of Chicago]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Landau |first=H. G. |year=1953 |title=On dominance relations and the structure of animal societies: III The condition for a score structure |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02476378 |journal=The Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics |language=en |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=143–148 |doi=10.1007/BF02476378 |issn=0007-4985|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Later, he moved to [[Columbia University]], again as a research associate, after being forced to leave [[Chicago]] by the [[House Un-American Activities Committee]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rashevsky |first=N. |year=1967 |title=Hyman Garshin Landau: December 18, 1909–December 2, 1966 |journal=The Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics |language=en |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=189–190 |doi=10.1007/BF02476972 |issn=0007-4985|doi-access=free }}</ref>
